Safe permissions are set in the PVWA or the PrivateArk Client, can be given to users **or** groups, and are inherited by group members. This distinction is examined repeatedly.
wrong: B, C and D each get one half backwards. The practical consequence of the real rule: always grant Safe permissions to groups, because permissions assigned directly to a user are lost if that user is ever deleted and recreated.

q: A leaver's LDAP-mapped Vault user is deleted in the PrivateArk Client, but the user reappears the next day. Why, and what is the correct action?
opts: A backup restore recreated the user; restore again from an earlier point

The user still exists in the directory and still matches a Directory Mapping, so they are recreated at their next authentication — remove them from the mapped LDAP group or disable the directory account instead
The Vault caches deleted users for 24 hours before purging them
AutoSyncExternalObjects must be disabled first
why: Transparent (LDAP) users are provisioned on demand. Deleting the Vault object removes the local record, not the eligibility — as soon as the person authenticates again and still matches a mapping, the user is recreated. The fix belongs in the directory: remove them from the mapped group, or disable the account. And note what deletion costs you: any Safe permissions assigned to that user individually are gone, while group-derived permissions come straight back.
wrong: A and C invent mechanisms. D — AutoSyncExternalObjects governs synchronisation of external objects on a schedule, and disabling it does not stop on-demand provisioning at logon.

q: A Directory Mapping specifies a User Template. When is that template applied?
opts: Every time a mapped user logs on, so template changes propagate to everyone
Only at the user's first authentication — later changes to the template do not retroactively affect users who already exist
When the CPM next completes a processing loop
Never; the template is documentation only
why: The User Template supplies the initial properties — authentication method, group memberships, Vault authorizations, restrictions — at the moment the transparent user is first created. After that the user is an independent object, so editing the template changes what *future* users get, not what existing ones have.
wrong: A is the intuitive assumption and the reason this is examined: administrators change a template expecting a fleet-wide update and get nothing. C and D are unrelated to the mechanism.

q: Which built-in user is the only one able to configure the LDAP integration and edit Directory Mappings?
opts: Master
Administrator
Auditor
DR
why: The **Administrator** user holds full Vault authorizations, installs the components, and is the only user who can configure LDAP integration and edit Directory Mappings. This is a favourite recall question.
wrong: A — the Master user has full, unremovable authorizations but is a break-glass identity: PrivateArk Client only, from the Vault console or the EmergencyStationIP, requiring the Master password and the Recovery private key. It is not for day-to-day configuration. C holds only the Audit Users authorization. D is the disaster-recovery user, an automatic owner of every Safe with Backup All Safes and Restore All Safes.

q: CyberArk Vendor PAM (Remote Access) is best described as:
opts: An on-premises VPN concentrator dedicated to third parties

A SaaS service giving external third parties privileged access on Zero Trust principles — biometric MFA through the CyberArk Mobile app and just-in-time provisioning, with no VPN, no agent and no vendor password
A drop-in replacement for the PSM
A reporting add-on for the PVWA
why: Vendor PAM is Remote Access bundled with PAM (Self-Hosted or Privilege Cloud). Remote Access itself is a SaaS service combining Zero Trust access, biometric authentication and just-in-time provisioning for remote vendors, consultants and maintenance personnel — the point being that the vendor needs no VPN, no installed agent and no credential of their own.
wrong: A describes the legacy approach it replaces. C — it works **with** the PSM, brokering the vendor's session through it. D understates it entirely.

q: Which component of Remote Access sits inside the customer's network and holds the secure data keys and certificates?
opts: The CyberArk Mobile app
The Remote Access Connector — a container deployed behind the firewall, which also acts as a SAML identity provider and runs the VendorLDAP directory used to provision vendor users
The Remote Access cloud tenant
The PVWA
why: The connector is what keeps the customer in control of their own secrets. It runs behind the firewall, holds the secure data keys and unique private certificates, acts as a SAML IdP, and runs a standalone OpenLDAP directory (VendorLDAP) whose certificate is installed on the Vault machine — a "VendorLDAP <site name>" directory then appears in the PVWA, and Directory Mappings map vendor users and groups to Vault objects, Safes and authentication methods.
wrong: A performs the biometric authentication. C orchestrates between the app and the connector but deliberately does not hold customer secrets. D is the PAM web interface. Note the fourth component: an internally deployed HTML5 Gateway that converts the inbound web protocol to outbound RDP over TLS.

q: How does a vendor authenticate to Remote Access, and where is the biometric data held?
opts: A password plus SMS one-time code; biometric templates are stored in the cloud tenant
Biometric authentication in the CyberArk Mobile app, enrolled with a unique, one-time, time-limited QR code — the biometric data stays on the phone and is never sent to or stored in the cloud service
A smart card issued by the customer's PKI
An LDAP password checked against the customer's Active Directory
why: Enrolment is a one-time, time-limited QR code scanned with the CyberArk Mobile app; thereafter the vendor authenticates biometrically on their own device. The biometric never leaves the phone and is never stored in the cloud service — which is what makes the model deployable across vendors without a credential-issuance process.
wrong: A is a conventional MFA design and is not how this works — and the claim about cloud-stored biometrics is specifically wrong. C would require issuing hardware to every third party. D would require creating directory accounts for vendors, which the whole design avoids.

q: A vendor connects through Vendor PAM to a Windows server. What happens to the target's credential?
opts: It is emailed to the vendor for the duration of the engagement

The vendor never receives it — the session is brokered through the portal to the PSM via the internally deployed HTML5 Gateway, so the credential stays in the Vault and the session is isolated, monitored and recorded
The vendor's own directory account is used instead
It is stored in the Remote Access cloud tenant for the session
why: This is the whole value proposition. Remote Access handles who the vendor is and whether they should have access right now; PAM handles the credential. The vendor lands in the PVWA or Privilege Cloud portal and connects through the PSM, so the credential is injected, never displayed, and the session is isolated, recorded and auditable exactly like an employee's.
wrong: A defeats the purpose. C would require provisioning directory accounts for third parties — the thing JIT provisioning exists to avoid. D is specifically not how it works: the connector keeps keys and certificates on the customer side, and the credential never leaves the Vault.
ref: Connect to targets using Remote Access

q: PTA-driven Continuous Accounts Discovery can automatically onboard an unmanaged privileged account it sees being used. Which target types does it support out of the box?
opts: Windows only
Windows, UNIX, AWS and Azure — anything else needs a custom PTA plug-in
Any platform that exists in the Vault
Only cloud platforms
why: Continuous discovery is PTA noticing a connection made with a privileged account that is not stored in the Vault, and reacting. Out of the box that detection-and-onboard path covers Windows, UNIX, AWS and Azure; extending it to anything else means writing a custom PTA plug-in. PTA also continuously monitors Windows local Administrators groups for newly privileged accounts.
wrong: A is too narrow, C too broad, D omits the two on-premises platforms that make up most of the value.

q: When an onboarding rule is created through the REST API, which filter is mandatory?
opts: `UserNameFilter`
`SystemTypeFilter` — Windows or Unix
`AddressFilter`
`IsAdminIDFilter`
why: `SystemTypeFilter` is the one mandatory filter, alongside the mandatory targets `TargetPlatformId` and `TargetSafeName`. Everything else — username, address, machine type, account category — is optional narrowing.
wrong: A, C and D are all real optional filters. `UserNameFilter` is capped at 512 characters and pairs with `UserNameMethod`; `AddressFilter` pairs with `AddressMethod`; `IsAdminIDFilter` is a boolean.

q: An onboarding rule's `UserNameMethod` and `AddressMethod` accept which values?
opts: Equals, Begins, Ends
Contains, Regex, Exact
Include, Exclude
StartsWith, EndsWith, Wildcard
why: Both matching methods take Equals, Begins or Ends. That is deliberately simple — rules are meant to be predictable and auditable, so there is no regular-expression matching here.
wrong: B, C and D all offer richer matching than the rule engine actually supports. Note the contrast with `AllowedSafes` on a platform, which *is* a regular expression — do not mix the two up.

q: Which values can an onboarding rule's Machine type and Account category filters take?
opts: Machine type: Any / Workstation / Server. Account category: Any / Privileged / Non-privileged
Machine type: Windows / Unix. Account category: Local / Domain
Machine type: Physical / Virtual. Account category: Service / Interactive
Machine type: Server / Endpoint. Account category: Tier 0 / Tier 1 / Tier 2
why: `MachineTypeFilter` is Any, Workstation or Server; `AccountCategoryFilter` is Any, Privileged or Non-privileged. Together with system type and a keyword these are what let you route, say, privileged accounts on servers into one Safe and workstation accounts into another.
wrong: B confuses machine type with system type. C and D invent categories that do not exist in the rule dialog.

q: You want a Windows discovery to run every week rather than once. Where is that set?
opts: It cannot be — discovery is always a one-off and must be re-run manually
In the Accounts Discovery definition itself, which supports a one-time scan or a recurring schedule
With a Windows scheduled task on the CPM server calling the scanner binary
In the Master Policy
why: Recurrence is part of the discovery definition in the PVWA. Making the scan recurring is what turns discovery from a one-off inventory exercise into an ongoing control, so newly created privileged accounts keep surfacing in Pending Accounts.
wrong: A and C describe workarounds for a capability that is built in. D is unrelated — the Master Policy governs access workflows, not discovery.

q: Which permission does a user need to obtain a copy of an SSH private key stored in the Vault?
opts: Use Accounts
List Accounts
Retrieve Accounts
Initiate CPM account management operations
why: An SSH private key is retrieved exactly like a password: List Accounts to see it, Retrieve Accounts to get a copy of the secret itself. This is why the same split-workflow logic applies — a user who only needs to connect gets Use, not Retrieve.
wrong: A gives Connect through the PSM, not the key material. B only reveals that the account exists. D exposes the Change / Verify / Reconcile buttons.
ref: Safe member permissions / SSH key management

q: Besides Windows Services, Scheduled Tasks and IIS Application Pools, which two dependency types can Windows discovery detect? (Choose two)
opts: IIS Anonymous Access
COM+ Applications
Registry keys holding credentials
ODBC connection strings
why: The discoverable set is Windows services, scheduled tasks, IIS application pools, IIS anonymous access and COM+ applications — all of them registered in a machine's own configuration surface, so they can be enumerated programmatically.
wrong: C and D are credentials embedded in arbitrary storage. The CPM can manage them once you add them by hand, but nothing can reliably find them by scanning.

q: Which onboarding sources use the "Add discovered accounts" REST method? (Choose three)
opts: The CPM Scanner
PTA
DNA (Discovery & Audit)
PARestore
why: "Add discovered accounts" is the ingestion path for anything that *discovers* — the CPM Scanner, PTA's continuous discovery, DNA and third-party scanners. Crucially, accounts arriving this way are evaluated against the automatic onboarding rules; accounts added with the plain "Add account" method are not.
wrong: D is a backup restore utility, not a discovery source.

q: Which statement about manually adding an account in the PVWA is correct?
opts: The address, username, platform and Safe are all required; the platform then determines which additional properties are mandatory
Only the username and password are required
The Safe is optional and defaults to PasswordManagerShared
The platform is chosen automatically from the address
why: Every account needs a location on the network (address), an identity (username), a Safe to live in and a target account platform to be governed by. The platform then dictates the rest — some platforms add mandatory properties such as a port, database name or domain.
wrong: B omits the two structural requirements. C and D are wrong: neither Safe nor platform is ever inferred, because both are deliberate access-control and policy decisions.

q: PTA has detected an unmanaged AWS IAM access key in use. Which automatic remediation actions can PTA take? (Choose three)
opts: Onboard the unmanaged account into the Vault
Rotate the credential
Reconcile the credential
Delete the IAM user
why: PTA's automatic containment set is onboard, rotate and reconcile — bringing the credential under management and invalidating whatever the attacker may hold. For AWS specifically it detects unmanaged access keys and passwords for IAM accounts, compromised privileged IAM accounts and compromised EC2 accounts.
wrong: D is destructive and outside PTA's remit — containment is about taking control of the credential, not deleting the identity. Where PSM is integrated, PTA can also suspend or terminate a live session.

q: Which onboarding path evaluates accounts against the automatic onboarding rules?
opts: "Add account" in the PVWA
"Add multiple accounts from a file" (bulk CSV upload)
"Add discovered accounts" — the path used by the CPM Scanner, PTA and DNA
Restoring a Safe with PARestore
why: Onboarding rules exist to triage *discovered* accounts. Only accounts arriving through the discovery ingestion path are compared against them; if none matches, the account lands in Pending Accounts for a human to place.
wrong: A and B are both deliberate acts where the operator has already chosen the Safe and platform, so there is nothing for a rule to decide. D is a restore operation.

q: What must the first row of a bulk-upload CSV contain?
opts: The Safe name that all accounts will go into
A header row of account property names
A count of the accounts in the file
The platform ID
why: The first row is a header naming the properties each column carries, so the upload can map columns to account properties — including platform-specific ones. Downloading the sample CSV from the Add accounts from file window is the reliable way to get the header right.
wrong: A and D are per-account column values, not file-level headers — different rows can target different Safes and platforms. C is not part of the format.
ref: Add multiple accounts from a file

q: Before an onboarding rule that references a reconcile account can run successfully, what must be true?
opts: The reconcile account must already exist, per the rule's definition, alongside the target Safe
The CPM will create the reconcile account on first use
Reconcile accounts cannot be referenced by onboarding rules
The reconcile account must be in the Pending Accounts list
why: The documented prerequisite is to create the Safe *and* the reconcile account according to the rule's definition before the rule runs. A rule places accounts into a prepared structure; it does not build the structure.
wrong: B — nothing is auto-created. C is false. D confuses a working reconcile account with a discovered one.

q: Which of these best describes how CyberArk now recommends sequencing an onboarding programme?
opts: Onboard the largest account populations first to show rapid coverage numbers
Work through a risk-versus-effort prioritisation — highest risk reduction for lowest implementation effort first
Follow the five Blueprint stages in strict order
Onboard alphabetically by Safe name so nothing is missed
why: The Blueprint's five-stage model was retired in August 2024 and replaced by a risk-effort index: a prioritisation matrix weighing the risk impact of a use case against the effort to implement it. In practice that still puts Tier 0 first, but the framing is now explicitly about return on effort rather than a fixed sequence.
wrong: A optimises for a metric that does not reduce risk. C is the retired model — still taught in v12.6 material, so know it exists, but know it has been superseded. D is arbitrary.

q: Which statement about discovered SSH keys is correct?
opts: They are discovered by Windows discovery
UNIX discovery returns them along with local accounts, including the trust relationships between machines
They can only be added manually
They are stored outside the Vault, on the CPM
why: UNIX discovery enumerates local accounts and SSH keys, and mapping the authorized/trusted key relationships is often the more valuable output — key-based trust paths are exactly how an attacker moves laterally across a UNIX estate.
wrong: A — Windows discovery has no SSH keys to find. C is false. D is false: keys are vaulted objects, protected like any other secret. Note that once a key is imported it should be rotated immediately, because the act of entering it exposed it.
ref: Accounts Discovery — UNIX / onboard SSH keys

q: Which ports does PTA use to communicate with the Vault and the DR Vault?
opts: TCP 443 only
TCP and UDP 1858
TCP 9022
UDP 514
why: PTA needs both TCP and UDP on 1858 to the Vault and to the DR Vault — it consumes the Vault's activity stream as well as making requests. Administrator access to the PTA itself is over TCP 80/443.
wrong: A is the PVWA's user-facing port. C is the Remote Control Client to PARAgent. D is syslog, which is how PTA *receives* logs from other sources, not how it talks to the Vault.

q: PVWA-to-PTA calls have started failing. Which account is involved, and what is the documented remedy?
opts: `PVWAGWUser` — recreate its credential file
`PTA_PAS_Gateway` — re-sync the PTA Vault users by running `VaultPermissionsValidation.sh` in the PTA server's utility folder
`PasswordManager` — reset its password in the PrivateArk Client
`Backup` — enable the user and set a password
why: `PTA_PAS_Gateway` is the account used for REST calls between the PVWA and PTA. When that link breaks, the fix is to re-synchronise the PTA Vault users and that account by running `VaultPermissionsValidation.sh` from the utility folder on the PTA server — reachable with the `UTILITYDIR` alias.
wrong: A is the PVWA's gateway impersonation user. C is the CPM's user. D is the backup user used by PAReplicate.

q: From version 14.0 onwards, where are PTA settings configured?
opts: Only on the PTA appliance's own console
In the PVWA interface
In `dbparm.ini` on the Vault
In the PrivateArk Client
why: Version 14.0 moved PTA settings into the PVWA, alongside CIS Level 2 hardening on RHEL 8, event closure reasons and richer email notifications carrying Event and Session IDs. It is a good example of the general direction: configuration consolidating into the web interface.
wrong: A was the older model. C configures the Vault, not PTA. D manages Vault users, groups and Safes.

q: What is the purpose of listing more than one address in a component's `Vault.ini`?
opts: Load balancing across multiple production Vaults
Failover — the component tries the next address if the first is unreachable, which is how components find the DR Vault after a failover
Replication configuration
Specifying the PVWA and the Vault together
why: `Vault.ini` holds the Vault's address and port, and multiple addresses can be listed comma-separated. On failover the component works down the list, which is what lets CPMs, PVWAs and PSMs reattach to the DR Vault without being reconfigured by hand.
wrong: A — the Vault is not load balanced this way. C is `PADR.ini`. D — the PVWA is not referenced in Vault.ini.

q: A task requires setting a Vault-level authorization and creating a Network Area. Which interface do you use?
opts: The PVWA
The PrivateArk Client
PACLI
The Remote Control Client
why: The PrivateArk Client is the administrative interface for Vault-level objects: users and their Vault authorizations, groups, Network Areas, Safe properties such as the Restrictions tab, and Safe renaming. The PVWA is the day-to-day interface for accounts, Safes membership, platforms and policy.
wrong: A does not expose Network Areas. C is a scripting interface to Vault data. D controls Vault services remotely over 9022.

q: Which component sends email notifications from the Vault, and which Safe supports it?
opts: The PVWA, using `PVWAConfig`
The ENE (Event Notification Engine), using the `Notification Engine` Safe
The CPM, using `PasswordManagerShared`
PTA, using `VaultInternal`
why: The Notification Engine is one of the three Safes created at Vault installation — `Notification Engine`, `System` and `VaultInternal` — and the ENE service uses it to hold notification configuration and templates. It relays over SMTP on port 25, and writes `ENEConsole.log` and `ENETrace.log`.
wrong: A, C and D each name a real Safe belonging to a different component. `PVWAConfig` holds `PVConfiguration.xml` and `Policies.xml`; `PasswordManagerShared` holds platform definitions.

q: Which file holds the Vault's SNMP settings, and which parameters would you set there?
opts: `dbparm.ini` — `Syslog`, `SyslogServerIP`
`paragent.ini` — `SNMPHostIP`, `SNMPTrapPort`, `SNMPCommunity`
`tsparm.ini` — `SNMPTarget`
`my.ini` — `Server-id`
why: `paragent.ini` configures the Remote Control Agent, and SNMP trap delivery is part of that agent's job — hence `SNMPHostIP`, `SNMPTrapPort` and `SNMPCommunity` living there rather than in the main Vault configuration.
wrong: A is where syslog/SIEM forwarding is configured — a different monitoring channel. C defines where the Safes are located on disk. D is database configuration.

q: Which statement about forwarding Vault audit data to a SIEM is correct?
opts: It is configured in `dbparm.ini` and sent over syslog, typically on port 514
It requires EVD to run on a schedule
It is configured in the PVWA under Reports
It uses the Remote Control Agent on 9022
why: Syslog forwarding is a Vault-level setting in `dbparm.ini`, streaming audit records continuously to the SIEM over port 514 (TLS, TCP or UDP). Like every `dbparm.ini` change it needs a Vault restart to take effect.
wrong: B describes EVD, which is a pull-based export for custom reporting rather than a continuous feed. C generates reports into `PVWAReports`. D is service control.

q: Why does CyberArk care about NTP configuration across PAM components?
opts: It is only cosmetic — log timestamps look neater
Clock skew breaks Kerberos authentication, certificate validation and the correlation of audit records across components
NTP is required for the Vault licence to validate
It controls the CPM processing interval
why: Time is load-bearing in a PAM deployment. Kerberos rejects tickets outside a tight clock skew window, certificate validity checks depend on accurate time, and any forensic reconstruction depends on Vault, CPM, PSM and target logs agreeing on when things happened. Windows components are typically pointed at a reliable source with `w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:… /syncfromflags:manual /reliable:YES /update`.
wrong: A trivialises a real dependency. C and D are invented.

q: What is the maximum size of a Distributed Vault deployment?
opts: Two servers — one primary and one DR
Six servers — one Primary and five Satellites
Ten servers in an active-active cluster
Unlimited, limited only by licence
why: A Distributed Vault tops out at six servers: one Primary plus five Satellites. Satellites serve read requests locally to reduce latency for geographically dispersed sites, while writes go to the Primary.
wrong: A describes a classic Vault plus DR pair. C confuses it with Cluster Vault, which is a two-node active-passive arrangement for local high availability. D is wrong — the limit is architectural.

q: You need deeper LDAP logging on the Vault. Which form does the `DebugLevel` entry in `dbparm.ini` take?
opts: A single number from 0 to 6
Named modules with levels, e.g. `DebugLevel=LDAP(14,15)` or `DebugLevel=PE(1),PERF(1)`
`DebugLevel=High`
`DebugLevel=Trace`
why: Vault debugging is per-module: you name the module and the levels you want, such as `PE(1),PERF(1)` for the policy engine and performance, or `LDAP(14,15)` for directory troubleshooting. That keeps `Trace.d0`–`Trace.d4` focused instead of drowning you in everything at once.
wrong: A is the CPM's `CPMDebugLevels` scale (0 none, 1 exceptions, 2 trace, 3–6 CASOS). C is the PVWA's style. D is not a valid value. Remember the change needs a Vault service restart.

q: Which values do the PVWA's `DebugLevel` and `InformationLevel` settings take?
opts: 0 to 6
None, Low, High, Profiling
1 to 7
Yes / No
why: The PVWA uses named levels — None, Low, High and Profiling. Profiling is the heaviest and is for performance investigations rather than routine troubleshooting; leaving it on in production will fill the log folder quickly.
wrong: A is the CPM's scale. C is the PSM server trace range (the Recorder and Client sub-levels are 1–2). D is not a debug scale.

q: A PSM issue needs deeper tracing. Which statement about PSM `TraceLevels` is correct?
opts: There is a single level from 1 to 7 covering everything
The Server level runs 1–7, while the Recorder and Client levels each run 1–2
It is a Yes/No switch
It is set in the Master Policy
why: PSM tracing is split by subsystem: the PSM server itself has the widest range at 1–7, while the recorder and the client each have just two levels. Raising only the subsystem you suspect keeps the logs readable.
wrong: A misses the split. C describes the DR service's `EnableTrace=yes`. D is where access policy lives, not diagnostics.

q: Which two `PADR.ini` parameters determine how often the DR Vault replicates and how quickly it notices the production Vault is gone? (Choose two)
opts: `ReplicateInterval` — seconds between replications, default 3600
`CheckInterval` — seconds between availability checks, default 60
`EnableDbsync`
`AccessVaultForInactivity`
why: `ReplicateInterval` (3600 seconds, i.e. hourly) sets the data replication cadence. `CheckInterval` (60 seconds) is how often the DR service probes the production Vault; combined with `CheckRetriesCount` of 4 and a 30-second gap between retries, that is how long it takes before failover logic engages.
wrong: C controls database synchronisation and D controls whether the DR service accesses the Vault to test for inactivity — both real parameters, neither of which sets these two intervals. `EnableFailover` and `FailoverMode` govern whether failover happens at all.

q: Put the DR failover steps into the correct order.
opts: Start the PrivateArk Server → synchronise the database → start ENE → stop the DR service
Synchronise the database → start the PrivateArk Server → start ENE → stop the DR service
Stop the DR service → start the PrivateArk Server → synchronise the database → start ENE
Start ENE → synchronise the database → start the PrivateArk Server → stop the DR service
why: Synchronise first so the DR Vault holds the most complete data set available, then bring the Vault service up on that data, then start the notification engine, and only then stop the DR replication service — because while it is running it will keep trying to behave like a replica.
wrong: The other orders either start the Vault on unsynchronised data or stop the DR service before the Vault is serving, which is how people lose the last replication increment.

q: Production has been rebuilt and you are failing back from the DR Vault. What does the failback procedure require?
opts: Set `FailoverMode=No`, delete the last two lines of `PADR.ini` to force a full replication, and restart the DR service
Reinstall the DR Vault from scratch
Run `PARestore` against the production Vault
Nothing — failback is automatic once production responds
why: The last two lines of `PADR.ini` hold the replication position. Removing them makes the DR service forget where it was and perform a full replication rather than an incremental one, which is what you want when the production Vault's data has been rebuilt or diverged. `FailoverMode=No` returns the DR to replica behaviour.
wrong: B is unnecessarily destructive. C restores Safes from backup files, a different operation. D is dangerous — automatic failback risks split brain.

q: Which two conditions must be met before `PAReplicate.exe` can take a Vault backup? (Choose two)
opts: The built-in `Backup` user must be enabled and given a password
A credential file for that user must exist, referenced with `/logonfromfile`
The Vault service must be stopped for the duration
The `DR` user must be suspended
why: The command form is `PAReplicate.exe vault.ini /logonfromfile user.ini /FullBackup`. The `Backup` user ships disabled and without a password, so enabling it and setting one is a genuine setup step people forget, and like every component it authenticates with a credential file.
wrong: C is false and is the point of the replicator — backups run against a live Vault. D would break disaster recovery. Note that restoring with `PARestore.exe` requires the Restore All Safes authorization.

q: Which authorization is required to restore a Safe with `PARestore.exe`?
opts: Backup All Safes
Restore All Safes
Manage Safe
Audit Users
why: Backup and restore are deliberately separate authorizations. Backup All Safes lets a user copy data out; Restore All Safes lets a user write data back in, which is the far more dangerous capability and is why the `DR` user holds both while the `Backup` user's role is narrower.
wrong: A permits the backup, not the restore. C is a Safe-level property permission. D is an audit authorization.

q: `DRNotificationThreshold = Yes, Yes, 2, 24, 30m`. What does the final value mean?
opts: Notifications stop after 30 minutes
The DR status is checked every 30 minutes
The first notification is sent after 30 minutes
Replication runs every 30 minutes
why: The fields are: monitor, notify, hours before the first notification, hours between subsequent notifications, and how often to check. The DR threshold is the one where that last value is expressed in **minutes** rather than hours — a deliberate difference from `BackupNotificationThreshold`, whose equivalent field is in hours.
wrong: A and C misread the position. D is `ReplicateInterval` in `PADR.ini`, a different setting in a different file.

q: Which statement about CPM log handling is correct?
opts: Logs grow indefinitely and must be truncated manually
Old logs are rotated into `Logs\Old`, with third-party plug-in logs going to `Logs\Old\ThirdParty`
All CPM logs are uploaded to the Vault for retention
Logs are written only to the Windows Event Log
why: The CPM rotates its own logs into `Logs\Old`, with per-plug-in logs archived under `Logs\Old\ThirdParty`. Worth knowing alongside this: third-party plug-in logs are not uploaded to the Vault, so if you need one for a support case you must collect it from the CPM server.
wrong: A ignores built-in rotation. C over-states what is uploaded. D is wrong — CyberArk components log to files.

q: After changing a PVWA configuration file on disk, what is the standard step to make IIS pick it up, and how do you confirm the service state?
opts: `iisreset /restart`, then `iisreset /status`
Restart the PrivateArk Server service
Run `CreateCredFile.exe`
Wait 20 minutes for the automatic refresh
why: The PVWA is an IIS application, so `iisreset /restart` reloads it and `iisreset /status` confirms the services came back. This is also the final step after PKI changes to `applicationHost.config`.
wrong: B restarts the Vault, which is unnecessary and disruptive. C rebuilds a credential file. D is the PVWA's periodic *configuration* refresh from the Vault — it does not reload files edited on the web server itself.

q: Which file and utility belong to a Cluster Vault deployment?
opts: `PADR.ini` and `PAReplicate.exe`
`ClusterVault.ini` and `StorageManager.exe`
`tsparm.ini` and `CAVaultManager`
`Basic_psm.ini` and `PSMHardening.ps1`
why: `ClusterVault.ini` carries the logical node names, the virtual IP, the peer and local public and private IPs, the `StorageIdentifier` and the `QuorumDiskIdentifier`. `StorageManager.exe` identifies the disks — `-q` for the quorum drive and `-s` for the shared storage drive, as in `StorageManager.exe -qE -sF`.
wrong: A belongs to DR replication. C is Vale storage location configuration and the Vault management utility. D is the PSM.

q: What is the relationship between the Master Policy and platforms?
opts: The Master Policy sets baseline access rules for the whole environment, and exceptions can be defined at platform level for populations that need different treatment
Platforms override the Master Policy automatically
The Master Policy applies only to Windows accounts
They are alternative configuration models — you use one or the other
why: The Master Policy is the single place where the organisation's baseline access rules are expressed — dual control, reason for access, exclusive access, one-time passwords, session monitoring and recording. Where one population genuinely needs different treatment, you add an exception scoped to a platform rather than weakening the baseline for everyone.
wrong: B inverts the model — an exception must be created deliberately, nothing overrides silently. C and D are wrong; the Master Policy is universal and works together with platforms.

q: Which of these are Master Policy rules rather than platform parameters? (Choose three)
opts: Require dual control password access approval
Enforce check-in/check-out exclusive access
Enforce one-time password access
`MinValidityPeriod`
why: The Master Policy expresses *what the organisation requires* of privileged access — approval, exclusivity, one-time use, session monitoring, recording, reason for access. Those are policy statements, so they live centrally.
wrong: D is a platform parameter that controls *how* the mechanism behaves — the number of minutes the CPM waits after retrieval before replacing a one-time password. Policy says "one-time"; the platform parameter says "after 60 minutes". Keeping that division clear answers a lot of exam questions.

q: You need dual control for production databases but not for test databases, and both use the same platform. What is the cleanest approach?
opts: Turn dual control off globally and rely on training
Duplicate the platform so production and test have their own, then apply the exception to the production platform
Move all databases into one Safe
Edit the built-in platform directly
why: Exceptions are scoped to a platform, so two different policies means two platforms. Duplicating the platform is the standard answer to "same system type, different policy" — it is the same reason you would split `LIN SSH 30` from `LIN SSH 90`.
wrong: A abandons the control. C makes the problem worse by merging populations that need different rules. D is not the way to customise, since built-in platforms are not meant to be edited and can be overwritten on upgrade.
ref: Master Policy exceptions / duplicate a platform

q: `EnforcePasswordVersionsHistory` is set to 7 on a platform. What does that mean?
opts: Seven password versions are retained in the Safe
The CPM will not reuse any of the last seven generated passwords
Passwords expire after seven days
Seven failed changes trigger an alert
why: This is password *history* enforcement — the CPM avoids regenerating any of the last seven values, mirroring the history rules the target operating system enforces itself. Valid values run 1–50, or -1 to disable.
wrong: A is Safe version retention, a Safe property ("save the latest N versions", default five). C and D are invented.

q: `RotationLatency` is documented as applying only in one circumstance. Which?
opts: Only when `HeadStartInterval` is 0
Only when the account uses one-time passwords
Only for UNIX platforms
Only during the FromHour/ToHour window
why: `RotationLatency` (default 0, range 0–60 minutes) introduces a small random delay so that a large population of accounts due at the same moment does not all rotate simultaneously. It only applies when `HeadStartInterval` is 0 — because a head start already spreads the work across days.
wrong: B, C and D are not the documented condition. This pairing is exactly the kind of interaction between two parameters that exam questions like to probe.

q: What do `FromHour` and `ToHour` control on a platform?
opts: The hours during which users may open the Safe
The window during which the CPM may perform password operations for accounts on that platform
The PSM session duration limit
The hours during which reports may be generated
why: They define the CPM's working window, so credential changes can be confined to a maintenance period rather than landing in the middle of a trading day. `ResetOveridesTimeFrame` (default Yes) lets an immediate reset ignore the window when something urgent is required.
wrong: A is the Safe's Restrictions tab in the PrivateArk Client — a different control that produces ITATS100E when breached. C and D are unrelated.

q: What does `ChangeNotificationPeriod` do, and what does -1 mean?
opts: The number of seconds before a change that a notification is issued in an Application Access Manager environment; -1 means no notification
The number of days before expiry that the CPM starts changing; -1 means immediate
The number of retries after a failed change; -1 means unlimited
The number of minutes between CPM loops; -1 disables the platform
why: It exists for application credentials: applications retrieving a credential through AAM need warning that the value is about to change so they can re-fetch rather than fail. Setting it to -1 turns notification off.
wrong: B is `HeadStartInterval`, which is in days. C is invented. D is `Interval`.

q: What does the CPM do during a password verification?
opts: It changes the password and confirms the new one works
It logs on to the target with the password stored in the Vault to confirm the two still match, and flags the account as unsynchronised if they do not
It reads the password hash from the target and compares it
It checks the password against the platform's complexity policy
why: Verification is a read-only health check: prove the stored credential still opens the door. If it does not, the account is flagged unsynchronised — and with `RCAutomaticReconcileWhenUnsynched = Yes` that flag is what triggers reconciliation.
wrong: A is a change. C is impossible — passwords are stored as one-way hashes on the target. D is a policy check, not a verification.

q: An account is marked to reset immediately, but the platform's `MinValidityPeriod` has not yet elapsed and the current time is outside `FromHour`/`ToHour`. What happens with default settings?
opts: The reset waits for both conditions
The reset proceeds — `ResetOveridesMinValidity` and `ResetOveridesTimeFrame` both default to Yes
The reset is cancelled and must be re-issued
Only the time frame is overridden
why: Both override parameters default to Yes precisely because an immediate reset usually means something has gone wrong — a suspected compromise, a departure, an incident. Making it wait for a maintenance window would defeat the purpose.
wrong: A and D assume defaults that are not the shipped ones. C is not a behaviour the CPM has.
ref: Automatic Password Management — Privileged Account Management

q: What is an account group used for?
opts: Grouping Safe members for permission assignment
Keeping several accounts synchronised on the same password value, for cases where the same credential must exist identically on multiple systems
Grouping platforms for reporting
Grouping accounts to be onboarded together
why: Account groups solve the case where several accounts must genuinely hold the same password — a clustered application, a set of appliances sharing a service identity — so the CPM changes them as a unit and keeps the value identical.
wrong: A is Vault groups. C and D describe things account groups are often confused with. Note the related but distinct construct: a *group platform* determines when the coordinated change happens, while each account keeps its own target platform for the change mechanics.

q: Which Safe permission puts the Change, Verify and Reconcile buttons in front of a user?
opts: Manage Safe
Initiate CPM account management operations
Retrieve Accounts
Use Accounts
why: That permission is what lets a Safe member trigger CPM work on demand rather than waiting for the scheduled loop. It is separate from being able to see or use the credential, which is the point of granular Safe permissions.
wrong: A governs Safe properties. C reveals the secret. D allows a PSM session. Note that a user can hold this without holding Retrieve — a genuinely useful separation for an operations team that must fix accounts without reading passwords.

q: What is Object Level Access Control (OLAC), and what should you know before enabling it?
opts: It restricts a Safe by IP address; it can be toggled freely
It allows permissions to be set on individual accounts within a Safe rather than only at Safe level — and once enabled on a Safe it cannot be disabled
It encrypts individual objects with separate keys; it is enabled by default
It limits the number of objects in a Safe; it is set at platform level
why: OLAC moves the access-control boundary from the Safe down to individual objects inside it. The catch that matters operationally is that it is a one-way switch — a Safe with OLAC enabled cannot have it turned off, so it is a design decision rather than something to experiment with in production.
wrong: A describes network areas and restrictions. C confuses it with the encryption hierarchy, where every object already has its own File Key. D is `MaxSafeSize` and object limits.

q: A contractor needs access to a Safe for a fixed six-week engagement. What is the cleanest control?
opts: Set a membership expiration date on their Safe membership
Set `FromHour`/`ToHour` on the platform
Create a Master Policy exception
Set the Safe's object retention to 42 days
why: Safe membership carries an expiration date, which is the built-in way to make temporary access actually temporary rather than depending on someone remembering to remove it. Better still, apply it to a group membership so the pattern is repeatable.
wrong: B restricts when the CPM operates. C changes access workflow, not duration. D governs how long objects are kept before deletion — nothing to do with who may reach them.

q: A CPM password change for a domain service account succeeds in Active Directory, but updating one of its dependent Windows Services fails. What is the practical consequence?
opts: Nothing — the service keeps running with the old password
The service will fail to start next time it restarts, because the credential it holds no longer matches the domain
The domain password is rolled back automatically
The account is deleted from the Safe
why: A running service holds its token already, so nothing appears broken until it restarts — which is what makes this failure mode dangerous: it surfaces at the next reboot or patch window, long after the change. This is why dependency handling and `SearchForUsages` matter, and why the CPM logs dependency failures separately.
wrong: A is true only until the next restart, which is precisely the trap. C — there is no automatic rollback. D does not happen.

q: What is a rotational group used for?
opts: Rotating the CPM that manages a Safe
Rotating through a set of accounts that serve the same purpose, so a freshly rotated credential is always available for the next user
Rotating recording Safes on a schedule
Rotating platform assignments between environments
why: Rotational groups exist for high-demand shared access: rather than one account being checked out, changed and unavailable, a pool of equivalent accounts is rotated so someone always has a ready credential. It is the fourth platform tab, alongside Targets, Dependents and Groups.
wrong: A is Safe-level CPM assignment. C and D are invented. Do not confuse it with a *group* platform, which changes several accounts together rather than cycling between them.

q: When you duplicate a platform, what is copied?
opts: The platform's settings only — accounts stay on the original platform until you move them
The settings and every account associated with the original
The settings and the Safe
Nothing — a duplicate starts from defaults
why: Duplication copies configuration, not data. Existing accounts remain associated with the original platform, and moving them is a separate deliberate action — which is what makes duplication safe to do in production while you prepare a new policy.
wrong: B would silently change the policy applied to live accounts. C — Safes are unrelated to platforms. D would defeat the purpose of duplicating.

q: Which statement about the CPM plug-in architecture is correct?
opts: Plug-ins run on the Vault
Each managed platform type uses a plug-in on the CPM that knows how to verify, change and reconcile on that target, and it writes its own log under `Logs\ThirdParty\`
Plug-ins are stored in the `System` Safe
There is one universal plug-in for all platforms
why: The CPM is a scheduler and a policy engine; the platform-specific knowledge of *how* to change a password on Oracle, or a Cisco appliance, or a Windows local account, lives in the plug-in. That separation is why the Marketplace can supply support for new target types without a CPM upgrade.
wrong: A — the Vault stores and protects, it does not connect to targets. C — platform definitions live in `PasswordManagerShared`; plug-ins are files on the CPM. D would make the Marketplace pointless.

q: An SSH key and a password for the same UNIX account are both to be managed. What must be true?
opts: They can share a Safe, but they need separate platforms
They must be in separate Safes and can share a platform
Both must use the `Unix via SSH` platform
SSH keys cannot be managed alongside passwords
why: The Safe is an access-control boundary and can hold both; the platform is the management policy, and password rotation and SSH key rotation are different mechanics, so each needs its own. Remember also that an imported key should be rotated immediately, because the act of entering it exposed it.
wrong: B reverses which one must be separate. C names the password platform only. D is false — SSH key management is a core capability.

q: Which of these is the strongest reason to grant Safe permissions to groups rather than to individual users?
opts: Groups process faster in the CPM
Individually-assigned permissions are lost if the user object is deleted and recreated — which happens routinely with LDAP-provisioned users
The Vault has a limit on individual permissions
Groups are required for reporting
why: Transparent (LDAP) users are provisioned on demand and can be deleted and recreated by ordinary lifecycle events. Permissions attached to the user object vanish with it; permissions derived from group membership come straight back. It also makes access reviews tractable — you review a handful of groups instead of thousands of individual grants.
wrong: A is not a real performance consideration. C and D are invented.

q: A platform's `AllowedSafes` is left at its default. What is that default and what does it mean?
opts: Empty — the platform cannot be used until Safes are named
`.*` — the platform can be used in any Safe, and the CPM searches all of them for accounts using it
`^PasswordManager` — only CPM Safes
`*` — all Safes, but only for Windows platforms
why: The default `.*` matches every Safe name. That is fine in a small deployment, but in a large one it means the CPM scans every Safe on every loop for every platform, which is a real performance cost — narrowing `AllowedSafes` is a standard CPM tuning step.
wrong: A would break the platform out of the box. C and D are invented values.

q: Approximately how many managed passwords can a single optimised CPM support, and what is one of the main levers for reaching that?
opts: 10,000; adding more Safes
100,000; tuning `AllowedSafes`, `Interval`, `MaxConcurrentConnections` and staggering `FromHour`/`ToHour` across platforms
1,000,000; increasing RAM
50,000; enabling OLAC
why: Around 100,000 is the figure to remember for a well-tuned CPM. Reaching it is about not wasting work: scoping platforms to the Safes that matter, spreading the load across the day rather than piling every change into the same hour, and controlling concurrency to each target.
wrong: A and D understate it and name irrelevant levers. C overstates it dramatically. OLAC is an access-control feature with no bearing on CPM throughput.

q: Why is "require users to specify a reason for access" more than a paperwork exercise?
opts: It slows users down, which reduces credential use

It attaches intent to each access event in the audit trail, so a later review can distinguish routine work from anomalous access — and it pairs with ticketing integration to tie access to an approved change
It prevents credential theft outright
It is required for the PSM to record
why: Audit records show that access happened; the reason field records why the person said they needed it. That is what makes review possible at scale, and with a ticketing system integrated the reason can be validated against a real change record rather than free text.
wrong: A is not the intent. C over-claims — it is a detective and deterrent control, not a preventive one. D is false; recording is governed by its own Master Policy rule.

q: Which statement about the Safe as a design unit is most accurate?
opts: Safes should be as large as possible to reduce administration
A Safe is the unit of access control, so its boundaries should follow who needs access — grouping accounts that share the same audience and the same owners
Each account should have its own Safe for maximum granularity
Safe design should follow the platform, one Safe per platform
why: Everything about a Safe — membership, permissions, the CPM assignment, retention, the audit scope of a report — applies to the whole Safe. So the right boundary is the population of people who should see the same things. Get that wrong and you spend the rest of the deployment fighting it, because the Safe model is the hardest thing to change later.
wrong: A collapses access control. C is unmanageable at any real scale, and OLAC exists precisely so you do not have to do this. D conflates policy with access — one platform is often used across many Safes.

q: An operations team needs to run Change and Verify on accounts but must never see the passwords. Which permission set delivers that?
opts: List Accounts + Initiate CPM account management operations, without Retrieve Accounts
List Accounts + Retrieve Accounts
Manage Safe
Use Accounts + Retrieve Accounts
why: The permissions are deliberately granular so this exact separation is possible: the team can see the accounts and trigger CPM operations on them, but the secret itself is never displayed to them. It is the same principle as the Use-versus-Retrieve split for session access.
wrong: B gives them the passwords. C gives Safe property administration and still not the operations buttons. D gives both a session and the credential.

q: What is the practical benefit of deactivating platforms you do not use?
opts: It reduces licence consumption
Better administration — deactivated platforms are hidden from users choosing a platform — and better performance, since the CPM does not process them
It frees space in the Vault
It is required before a platform can be deleted
why: Two benefits, and the exam wants both. Fewer platforms in the picker means fewer wrong choices at onboarding time; and every active platform is work the CPM schedules on every loop, so deactivating the unused ones is genuine tuning.
wrong: A — licensing counts managed accounts. C — platform definitions are tiny. D is invented. Note that deactivating a target platform also deactivates its dependent platforms.

q: What is the correct order of the Vault's hierarchical encryption?
opts: Server Key → Safe Key → File Key
File Key → Safe Key → Server Key
Recovery Key → File Key → Safe Key
Safe Key → Server Key → File Key
why: Every object is encrypted with its own File Key; the File Key is encrypted with the Safe Key; the Safe Key is encrypted with the Server Key. Reading it outward from the object is the reliable way to remember it: object → Safe → server. The consequence is that without the Server Key, nothing below it can be opened.
wrong: The other orders invert the hierarchy. The Recovery Key sits alongside rather than inside this chain: the Safe Key is *also* encrypted with the Recovery public key, so it can be recovered with the Recovery private key.

q: Which Server Key storage option is described as both strong and convenient, and why?
opts: An external medium such as a USB device removed after startup — strong but inconvenient
The local disk — convenient but weaker
An HSM — strong and convenient, because the key is used inside the module and is never held in the Vault server's memory
A network share protected by ACLs
why: The three options trade off along one axis. External media is strong because the key can be physically removed after the Vault starts, but that makes unattended restarts impossible. Local disk restarts cleanly but leaves the key on the machine. An HSM resolves the tension: the key never leaves the module, so it is neither on disk nor in the Vault's RAM.
wrong: A and B are correctly described but are not the both-strong-and-convenient option. D is not a supported model and would be weaker than local disk.

q: Where should the Recovery private key be stored?
opts: On the Vault server, alongside the Server Key
On physical media in at least two secure locations — typically the primary site and the DR site
In the `System` Safe
On the CPM server, protected by a credential file
why: The Recovery private key is the last resort for opening the Vault's data, so it must be both protected and available. Storing it on the Vault it protects would defeat the purpose; storing only one copy risks losing everything to a single site event. Two secure physical locations — primary and DR — is the documented practice.
wrong: A destroys the separation the key exists to provide. C is inside the very system being recovered. D is unrelated — credential files protect component authentication.

q: How is the Safe Key protected so that recovery is possible?
opts: It is stored in plaintext on the Vault
It is encrypted with the Server Key and also with the Recovery public key, so it can be recovered using the Recovery private key
It is derived from the Master user's password
It is stored in the `VaultInternal` Safe
why: Two independent paths to the same Safe Key: the normal operational path through the Server Key, and the break-glass path through the Recovery key pair. That dual encryption is exactly what makes Master-user recovery possible when the Server Key is lost, without weakening day-to-day protection.
wrong: A would make the whole hierarchy pointless. C and D are invented mechanisms.

q: PTA's detections fall into three families. Which set is correct?
opts: Malware, phishing and insider threat
Attacks that bypass security controls; statistical anomalies; Active Directory risks
Network, endpoint and cloud
Preventive, detective and corrective
why: Bypass detections cover abuse of privileged accounts whether or not CyberArk manages them — unmanaged privileged access, suspected credential theft, suspicious password change, suspicious in-session activity. Statistical anomalies use profiling to spot irregular hours, irregular source IPs, excessive access and dormant users waking up. AD risks are configuration weaknesses an attacker could abuse, flagged before they are abused.
wrong: A is generic security taxonomy. C describes data sources rather than detection families. D is a control classification.

q: Which PTA detections come from EPM (Endpoint Privilege Manager) rather than from the Vault, logs or AD? (Choose three)
opts: Suspected LSASS credentials harvesting
Suspected SAM hash harvesting
Suspected credentials theft from Chrome
Excessive access to privileged accounts in the Vault
why: The whole "harvesting / theft from <somewhere on the endpoint>" family comes from EPM, because those are endpoint memory and application events that only an endpoint agent can see — LSASS, SAM hashes, Chrome, Firefox, VNC, WinSCP, service accounts and cached domain credentials.
wrong: D is a Vault-behaviour anomaly derived from Vault activity. The memory hook is worth keeping: endpoint theft → EPM, Vault behaviour → Vault, delegation and SPN issues → AD.

q: Which of these are Active Directory risks that PTA proactively reports? (Choose three)
opts: Unconstrained Delegation
Risky SPN
Service account logged on interactively
Access to the Vault from an irregular IP address
why: These are configuration weaknesses that make an attacker's job easier, and PTA flags them so they can be fixed *before* they are exploited — which is a different value proposition from detecting an attack in progress. Dual Usage belongs to the same family.
wrong: D is a statistical anomaly derived from Vault activity, not an AD configuration risk.

q: A Privileged Session Analysis and Response rule is defined by which attributes?
opts: Category, Pattern (a regular expression), Session response, Threat Score and Scope
Safe, Platform, User and Action
Severity, Date and Event Type
Source IP, Destination IP and Port
why: Category selects what is being watched — SSH, Universal Keystrokes, SCP, SQL or Windows title. Pattern is the regular expression to match. Session response is Suspend, Terminate or None. Threat Score runs 1–100. Scope narrows the rule to particular Vault users, accounts or machines.
wrong: B and D describe other objects entirely. C are the filters used to review PTA events in the Security pane, not the fields that define a response rule. CyberArk recommends studying the predefined rule set first, then modifying and adding rules to fit the organisation.
ref: PTA — privileged session analysis and response

q: With PTA and PSM integrated, what changes for an audit team reviewing recordings?
opts: Recordings are compressed to save space
Each session is assigned a risk score, so reviewers can prioritise the riskiest sessions instead of sampling at random
Recordings are automatically deleted if no risk is found
Only failed sessions are recorded
why: This is the practical answer to "nobody can watch ten thousand hours of RDP". PTA analyses session activity and scores it, which turns review from random sampling into a ranked queue — and the same integration allows automatic suspension or termination during high-risk activity.
wrong: A, C and D are not behaviours of the integration, and C in particular would destroy audit evidence.

q: Which groups can see PTA security events in the PVWA, and where?
opts: Auditors, in the Privileged Sessions tab
Security Admins and Security Operators, in the Security pane
Vault Admins, in System Health
PVWAMonitor, in Reports
why: PTA events surface in the Security pane, which is scoped to Security Admins and Security Operators — a separate audience from the auditors reviewing recordings and the administrators managing the platform. Events are shown on a timeline and can be filtered by severity, event type and date.
wrong: A is where session recordings are reviewed. C shows component health. D is the reporting group. Each event card carries the last detection time, the event name, the score and severity, whether remediation has started, and the recommended or automatically taken action.

q: Which statement best captures the Vault's defence-in-depth design?
opts: A single strong firewall protects the Vault

The Vault runs a hardened, closed operating system with its own built-in firewall, no standard network services, no third-party access, and its own authentication and access control — several independent layers rather than one
Security is provided by the network team's segmentation
Encryption alone protects the data
why: The Digital Vault's premise is that no single control should be load-bearing. The server is hardened and closed to everything except the CyberArk protocol on its own firewall, the operating system is not available for general use, the Vault authenticates and authorises independently of the domain, and the data is encrypted hierarchically underneath all of it.
wrong: A, C and D each describe one layer and treat it as sufficient — which is exactly the assumption the design rejects.
ref: Vault security layers / Digital Vault Security Standard

q: Playback of a PSM recording through the PVWA depends on which group?
opts: `PSMLiveSessionTerminators`
`PVWAGWAccounts` — the gateway accounts that enable playback through the PVWA
`Safe Managers`
`Notification Engines`
why: `PVWAGWAccounts` are the gateway accounts with access to password Safes that make PVWA-mediated operations, including recording playback, possible. Alongside them, `PSMAppUsers` creates recording Safes and uploads recordings, `PSMMaster` manages those Safes, and `Auditors` get read access to all of them.
wrong: A suspends and terminates live sessions. C is a role name rather than a predefined group. D relates to the ENE.

q: An auditor wants a report of everything a specific user did, and separately everything that happened in a specific Safe. Which permissions are involved?
opts: Audit Users for the user-activity view; View Audit on the Safe for the Safe-activity view
Manage Users for both
List Accounts for both
Backup All Safes for both
why: The two questions have two different scopes and therefore two different permissions. "What did this person do?" spans the Vault and needs the Vault-level Audit Users authorization. "What happened in this Safe?" is bounded by the Safe and needs View Audit on it.
wrong: B is a user-administration authorization — the Entitlement report accepts either Manage Users or Audit Users, but Activity Log scope works as described above. C only reveals that accounts exist. D is for backups.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts a PSM connection with a PSM for SSH connection?
opts: Both always go through the PVWA
A PSM (Windows) session is normally launched from the PVWA, whereas PSM for SSH lets the user connect straight from a native SSH client without touching the web interface
PSM for SSH requires the HTML5 Gateway
Neither records the session
why: That is the point of PSM for SSH: administrators keep their own terminal and workflow, connecting with a single SSH command, while the session is still brokered, isolated, recorded and audited. The Windows PSM flow normally starts from the PVWA's Connect button.
wrong: A ignores the direct SSH path. C — the HTML5 Gateway fronts the Windows PSM for browser-based sessions. D is wrong: both record.
ref: PSM and PSM for SSH flows

q: Which PSM for SSH connection string is correct?
opts: `ssh targetaccount@vaultuser@psmaddress@targetaddress`
`ssh vaultuser@targetaccount@targetaddress@psmaddress`
`ssh psmaddress@vaultuser@targetaccount@targetaddress`
`ssh vaultuser@psmaddress@targetaccount@targetaddress`
why: Read it as a sentence: who you are (your Vault user), what you want to become (the target account), where you are going (the target address), and finally what you actually connect to (the PSM). The PSM address is last because it is the host your SSH client is really opening a session to.
wrong: The other orders scramble those four elements. Building the sentence in your head is more reliable at exam time than memorising the string.

q: Which connection components belong to PSM for SSH? (Choose three)
opts: `PSMP-SSH`
`PSMP-SCP`
`PSMP-SFTP`
`PSM-WinSCP`
why: The PSMP family covers the SSH world: `PSMP-SSH` for interactive sessions and `PSMP-SCP`, `PSMP-SFTP` and `PSMP-Rsync` for file transfer, all brokered and audited by PSM for SSH.
wrong: D is a Windows PSM connection component — WinSCP is a graphical Windows client launched inside a PSM session, which is a different mechanism from a native SSH file transfer through PSMP.

q: Estimate the recording storage for 30 days of retention, 250 sessions per day, 60 minutes per session, high-activity RDP.
opts: About 20 GB
About 155 GB
About 470 GB
About 2 TB
why: High-activity RDP is budgeted at 300 KB per minute. 30 days x 250 sessions x 60 minutes = 450,000 minutes; 450,000 x 300 KB = 135,000,000 KB, which is about 129 GB. The sizing formula then adds a constant 20 GB, giving roughly 150-155 GB.
wrong: Work it as sessions x minutes x rate x days, then add 20 GB. The rate is what usually goes wrong: memorise 100 / 200 / 300 KB per minute for SSH / low-activity RDP / high-activity RDP. Using 100 KB/min here would give about 63 GB; there is no arithmetic that reaches 470 GB or 2 TB at this volume.

q: You are sizing PSM servers for 240 concurrent sessions on virtual machines. How many servers should you plan for, before adding redundancy?
opts: Two — 100 sessions each with headroom
Four — the guideline is 100 concurrent sessions per PSM server, reduced by up to 40% on a VM, so budget around 60 per virtual server
One — a single PSM scales to 300
Six — 40 sessions per server
why: The published guideline is up to 100 concurrent sessions per PSM server, and virtualisation can cost up to 40% of that. At roughly 60 sessions per virtual server, 240 concurrent sessions needs four — and that is before you add capacity for failure of one node.
wrong: A applies the physical figure to virtual servers. C and D misremember the base number in opposite directions.

q: From version 14.4, what happens to a PSM recording that reaches 2 GB?
opts: The session is terminated
The recording is split automatically and continues in a new file
The recording is truncated and the rest is lost
The recording is compressed in place
why: Automatic splitting at 2 GB means very long sessions no longer produce a single unmanageable object, and nothing is lost. Before this, large recordings were a genuine operational problem for upload and playback.
wrong: A would disrupt legitimate work. C would destroy audit evidence — the exact thing recording exists to preserve. D is not the mechanism.

q: Which file and parameter define which users may connect to a PSM for SSH server for maintenance, bypassing the PSMP shell?
opts: `sshd_config` — `PSMP_MaintenanceUsers`
`basic_psmpserver.conf` — `AdminUsers`
`Basic_psm.ini` — `MaintenanceUsers`
`PSMHardening.ps1` — `$PSM_CONNECT_USER`
why: `PSMP_MaintenanceUsers` in `sshd_config` names the accounts allowed a normal shell on the PSM for SSH host, so administrators can still maintain the server itself without every SSH connection being intercepted and brokered.
wrong: B is the PSMP server's main configuration file but not where this is set. C is the Windows PSM's configuration. D is a Windows PSM hardening variable, alongside `$SUPPORT_WEB_APPLICATIONS`.

q: You have three PSM servers behind a load balancer. What must be true about recordings?
opts: Recordings stay on whichever PSM handled the session, so playback must be directed to that server
Recordings are uploaded to the Vault, so playback does not depend on which PSM served the session
Each PSM needs its own recording Safe named after it
Load balancing is not supported with recording enabled
why: Recordings are uploaded into Vault Safes, not left on the PSM host. That is what makes horizontal scaling straightforward — any PSM can serve any session and the audit trail lands in one governed place. It also means recording Safes inherit Vault protection and Safe-level access control.
wrong: A describes a pre-upload state only. C is possible with a dynamic `SessionRecorderSafe` value but is not a requirement. D is false.

q: Which PSM hardening script variables would you review when a PSM must support web application connection components?
opts: `$SUPPORT_WEB_APPLICATIONS` and `$PSM_CONNECT_USER` in `PSMHardening.ps1`
`AllowSelectHTML5` and `DefaultConnectionMethod`
`SessionRecorderSafe` and `SessionRecorderSafeRetention`
`AllowMonitor` and `AllowTerminate`
why: Hardening a PSM locks down the interactive session environment, and browser-based connection components need some of that relaxed in a controlled way. `$SUPPORT_WEB_APPLICATIONS` governs that, and `$PSM_CONNECT_USER` identifies the session user the hardening applies to.
wrong: B controls HTML5-versus-RDP delivery. C configures recording storage. D governs live monitoring. All real settings, none of them hardening variables.

q: Why should the Windows active-session and idle-session limits on a PSM server be set to Never?
opts: To let users stay connected as long as they like
Because a Windows-enforced disconnect can cut a session mid-write and corrupt the recording — session duration should instead be limited at platform level
Because AppLocker requires it
Because the HTML5 Gateway does not support timeouts
why: Windows session timeouts and PSM recording do not mix: an abrupt disconnect can leave a recording incomplete or corrupt. The right place to bound a session is the platform, where the limit is applied by the PSM itself and the recording is closed cleanly.
wrong: A misreads the intent — the point is not unlimited sessions, it is enforcing the limit in the right layer. C and D are invented.

q: When registering an HTML5 Gateway in the PVWA, which three values are required?
opts: ID, Address (FQDN) and Port
Username, password and certificate
Safe, platform and connection component
IP range, subnet mask and gateway
why: Registration under Options → Privileged Session Management → Add Configured PSM Gateway Servers takes an ID, the gateway's fully qualified domain name and its port (443). The ID is then referenced when you associate the gateway with a specific PSM server under that PSM's Connection Details.
wrong: B, C and D belong to other configuration objects. Remember the two-step nature: registering the gateway is not enough on its own — it must also be associated with a PSM server and enabled.
ref: Secure access with an HTML5 Gateway

q: A user connecting through the HTML5 Gateway reports the wrong keyboard layout. Which settings are relevant?
opts: `KeyboardLayout` and `ServerKeyboardLayout`, with `AllowLanguageSelection` / `AllowedLanguages` controlling what the user can pick
`DefaultConnectionMethod`
`PSMConnectionDefault`
`EnforceSubnetRules`
why: The gateway carries its own keyboard and language parameters because it is translating browser input into RDP. `KeyboardLayout` and `ServerKeyboardLayout` set the client and server sides, while `AllowLanguageSelection`, `AllowedLanguages` and `DisableLanguageSelection` decide how much choice the user gets.
wrong: B selects HTML5 versus an RDP file. C sets the default connection component for a platform. D restricts ad hoc connections by subnet.

q: During a live session an observer sees something suspicious but wants to investigate before cutting the user off. What is the appropriate action?
opts: Terminate the session immediately
Suspend the session — it can be resumed once the activity is understood, whereas termination is final
Change the account password
Delete the recording
why: Suspend and terminate are separate deliberately. Suspension freezes the session and preserves the ability to resume, which suits investigation; termination ends it. Both require membership of `PSMLiveSessionTerminators` and the corresponding server setting, and PTA response rules can trigger either automatically on a high-risk pattern.
wrong: A forecloses the investigation. C does not stop the session in progress. D destroys evidence.

q: Which statement about PSM text recording is correct?
opts: Text recording replaces video recording
Text, keystroke and command audit is captured alongside video, and it is what makes the recording archive searchable
Text recording is only available for SSH sessions
Text recordings are stored on the PSM server
why: The two are complementary. Video shows what the session looked like; the text and command audit is what an auditor can actually query — searching for a command across thousands of sessions rather than watching them. Windows sessions capture window titles and keystrokes; SSH sessions capture the command stream.
wrong: A treats them as alternatives. C is too narrow. D is wrong — recordings are uploaded to Vault Safes.

q: Which Safes are created by a PSM installation? (Choose three)
opts: `PSM`
`PSMLiveSessions`
`PSMUnmanagedSessions`
`PVWAReports`
why: The PSM's own Safe set includes `PSM`, `PSMLiveSessions`, `PSMNotifications`, `PSMRecordings`, `PSM Sessions`, `PSMUniversalConnectors` and `PSMUnmanagedSessions` — infrastructure for configuration, live session state, notifications, connectors and unmanaged ad hoc sessions.
wrong: D belongs to the PVWA's set, alongside `PVWAConfig`, `PVWAPrivateUserPrefs`, `PVWAPublicData`, `PVWATaskDefinitions`, `PVWATicketingSystem` and `PVWAUserPrefs`.

q: What is the security trade-off an administrator accepts when enabling ad hoc (Secure Connect) sessions?
opts: Sessions are not recorded
The credentials used are supplied at connect time and are not vaulted, so part of the PSM's security benefit — a secret the user never possesses — is lost
The PSM cannot isolate the session
Ad hoc sessions bypass AppLocker
why: Isolation and recording still apply, so the session is still brokered through the hardened PSM and still audited. What is lost is credential management: the user has and types the password, so it is neither rotated, nor unique, nor unknown to them. That is why ad hoc access should be scoped to named users or groups and, ideally, treated as a stepping stone to proper onboarding.
wrong: A and C are false — ad hoc sessions are recorded and isolated. D is false and would be a serious hardening gap.

q: Which parameter sets the default connection component offered for a platform, and where does it live?
opts: `PSMConnectionDefault`, under the platform's UI & Workflows → Connection Components
`DefaultConnectionMethod`, under Privileged Session Management UI
`PSMServerID`, under the Safe's properties
`AllowSelectHTML5`, on the connection component
why: `PSMConnectionDefault` names the component that appears pre-selected in the connect drop-down on the Account Details page — useful when a platform has several enabled components and one is the normal choice.
wrong: B decides HTML5 versus an RDP file, not which component runs. C is not a Safe property — PSM server association is set at platform level. D lets the user choose the connection method for a component. All four are real settings, which is what makes this a good discrimination question.

q: In Privilege Cloud, how does an Active Directory user end up with the right permissions on first login?
opts: An administrator creates the user manually in the portal beforehand
Role Mappings associate AD groups with Privilege Cloud roles, and any AD user in a mapped group is automatically assigned the matching role on first login
Every AD user gets the Privilege Cloud Users role by default
Permissions come from the Vault's Directory Mappings, exactly as in self-hosted
why: Role Mappings are the SaaS equivalent of transparent user provisioning: `CyberArk Vault Admins@acme.corp` maps to Privilege Cloud Administrators, `CyberArk Safe Managers@…` to Privilege Cloud Safe Managers, and so on. The user is assigned to the role the first time they log in.
wrong: A defeats the point of directory-driven provisioning. C would be a serious over-grant. D names the self-hosted mechanism — in Privilege Cloud the Identity layer does this. Note each role exists in standard, Basic and Lite versions; pick the standard one unless you specifically need the others.

q: In CyberArk Identity, what is the relationship between Authentication Profiles and Policy Sets?
opts: An Authentication Profile defines the MFA challenge chain; a Policy Set associates roles with an Authentication Profile
A Policy Set defines the challenges; an Authentication Profile assigns them to users
They are two names for the same object
Policy Sets apply only to service accounts
why: An Authentication Profile is the *what* — Challenge 1 might be Password and Challenge 2 an SMS confirmation code. A Policy Set is the *who* — it assigns specified roles and sets the default profile they must satisfy. Splitting them means one profile can serve several roles.
wrong: B reverses the two. C ignores a real separation. D is invented — Policy Sets are how ordinary users get their MFA requirements.
ref: Privilege Cloud — Authentication Profiles and Policy Sets

q: You are about to install a Privilege Cloud Connector and the installation fails to authenticate. What should you check first?
opts: The Vault's `dbparm.ini`
The `installeruser` password — it expires every 24 hours and must be reset before each install session
The CPM's credential file
The Master user's Recovery key
why: `installeruser` is the built-in Identity service account used during every component installation, and its password deliberately expires every 24 hours. If your install session is a day after you set it, it has already expired. Reset it under Core Services → Users → Set All Service Users before starting.
wrong: A is a self-hosted Vault file you do not control in Privilege Cloud. C is created *during* installation. D is a break-glass recovery artefact.

q: Which Privilege Cloud prerequisite is easy to miss and blocks Connector deployment?
opts: Registering the Connector machines' IP addresses in the tenant's IP allowlist
Installing the PrivateArk Client on each Connector
Opening port 1858 to the internet
Creating a DR Vault
why: Privilege Cloud requires the IP addresses of machines running Connectors to be registered in the tenant's IP allowlist, under Administration → Advanced Settings. CIDR notation is accepted, and propagation can take up to ten minutes — so it is worth doing before you need it rather than while an installer is waiting.
wrong: B is not required. C would be a serious exposure — the Vault is CyberArk-hosted. D is not part of Connector deployment.

q: Which description of Secure Infrastructure Access (SIA) is correct?
opts: An agent-based replacement for the PSM on Windows targets

A non-intrusive, agentless SaaS solution giving VPN-less access to Windows, Linux, databases and Kubernetes, using native clients over an MFA-secured connection, with either zero standing privileges or vaulted credentials
